title: 10 History Facts That Sound Fake (But Are 100% Real)
intro: Ten facts from history that sound like somebody made them up. Every one is checked against a museum, a university or a major newspaper, and the sources are in the description. We start with Cleopatra and the Moon landing, and we finish with a pharaoh who was buried holding a blade that came from outer space. Let's go.

segments.heading: Cleopatra was closer to the Moon landing than the pyramids
segments.text: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid. It sounds wrong, so here are the numbers. The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around twenty-five hundred BC, give or take a few decades. Cleopatra, the last queen of Egypt, died in thirty BC. That's a gap of about two and a half thousand years. Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon in 1969, which is just under two thousand years after Cleopatra. So from where she stood, the pyramids were older than she is to us. When she looked at them, she was looking at ancient ruins, the way we look at the Roman Colosseum. Ancient Egypt wasn't one era. It was a civilisation that lasted so long, it had its own ancient history. Cleopatra was a tourist at the pyramids, just like you'd be.

segments.heading: The fax machine is older than the telephone
segments.text: The fax machine was invented before the telephone. Not after. Before. In 1843, a Scottish clockmaker named Alexander Bain built what he called the electric printing telegraph. It used a stylus on a swinging pendulum to scan a flat surface line by line and send the pattern down a telegraph wire. The pictures were rough, but they worked. By 1863, an Italian inventor, Giovanni Caselli, was running a commercial fax service between Paris and Lyon, after showing Napoleon the Third that it could send a signature down the line. Alexander Graham Bell didn't get his telephone patent until March 1876. That's thirty-three years later. So you could send someone a fax a decade before the American Civil War, but you couldn't call to tell them it was coming. The office machine everyone thinks is obsolete is actually one of the oldest ideas in communication.

segments.heading: Nintendo is as old as the Eiffel Tower
segments.text: Nintendo was founded in 1889, the same year the Eiffel Tower opened. Nintendo's own company history records that in 1889, a man named Fusajiro Yamauchi began making and selling Japanese playing cards, called hanafuda, in a shop in Kyoto. The Eiffel Tower was inaugurated in Paris in March of that same year. So the company behind Mario is as old as the most famous tower on Earth. Nintendo stayed a playing-card company for decades. It made the first Western-style playing cards in Japan in 1902, and it didn't launch its first home video game machines until 1977. The Famicom, known outside Japan as the Nintendo Entertainment System, arrived in 1983. That means Nintendo spent its first ninety years with no screens at all. The next time somebody calls video games a young industry, remind them the company behind them was already old when the First World War started.

segments.heading: Chicago lifted its whole downtown with jacks
segments.text: In the 1850s, Chicago raised its entire downtown off the ground with jackscrews. The city was built on a marsh barely above the level of Lake Michigan, so sewage had nowhere to go. In 1854, cholera killed one in twenty Chicagoans. Instead of abandoning the city, the council decided to build sewers on top of the streets and lift everything up to meet them. Starting in 1856, crews slid hundreds of screw jacks under a building, then turned them a notch at a time. A young cabinet maker called George Pullman put six thousand jacks under a whole block of Lake Street, hired six hundred men, and raised the block over four days, with shops open and customers inside. Some buildings went up as much as fourteen feet. The job took nearly twenty years. Chicago quite literally picked itself up out of the mud, and the people inside kept drinking their coffee.

segments.heading: The first speeding ticket was for 8 miles an hour
segments.text: The first person ever fined for speeding was doing eight miles an hour. On the twenty-eighth of January 1896, Walter Arnold drove his Benz motor car through the village of Paddock Wood in Kent, England, at four times the legal limit. The limit was two miles an hour. A policeman spotted him, jumped on his bicycle, and chased him for about five miles before catching up. Arnold was charged on four counts, including using a locomotive without a horse and failing to have a man walking in front with a red flag. He was fined, and the speeding part cost him ten shillings. Guinness World Records lists it as the first speeding conviction in history. Later that same year, the law was changed and the limit went up to fourteen miles an hour. The red flag was dropped too. The policeman on the bicycle, presumably, got a rest.

segments.heading: A polar bear used to fish in the River Thames
segments.text: In the thirteenth century, a polar bear went fishing in the River Thames on a leash. The Tower of London was a royal zoo for six hundred years, and the charity that runs it, Historic Royal Palaces, keeps the records. It started in 1235, when the Holy Roman Emperor sent King Henry the Third three big cats, probably lions. In 1252, the King of Norway sent him a white bear, almost certainly a polar bear. It was kept muzzled and chained, but it was allowed into the river, tied to a long stout cord, to swim and catch its own fish. Three years later, the King of France sent an elephant, which got its own house and keeper. The menagerie ran until 1831, when two tigers killed a lion and King William the Fourth had the animals moved to Regent's Park, which became London Zoo. London's first zoo was a castle, and its star attraction caught its own dinner.

segments.heading: America banned sliced bread
segments.text: In 1943, the United States government banned sliced bread. On the eighteenth of January, Claude Wickard, the Secretary of Agriculture, ordered bakeries to stop slicing. The country was at war, and the reasoning was that sliced loaves need a thicker wax paper wrapping to stay fresh, so the ban would save paper, and also the steel that went into slicing machines. The public hated it. One woman wrote to the New York Times that sliced bread was vital to the morale and saneness of a household, because she had to hand-cut more than twenty slices every morning. Within a week, the Mayor of New York said bakeries could keep using the machines they already had. By the eighth of March, less than two months in, the government gave up. Wickard admitted the savings were smaller than expected. Sliced bread had only existed since 1928, and America had already decided it couldn't live without it.

segments.heading: A city danced for a month in 1518
segments.text: In the summer of 1518, hundreds of people in one city danced for weeks, and nobody could make them stop. It began on the fourteenth of July in Strasbourg, then part of the Holy Roman Empire. A woman known as Frau Troffea stepped into the street and started dancing. She danced until she collapsed, then got up the next day and carried on. Within a week, more than thirty people had joined her. Within a month, about four hundred. Some accounts claim dancers died of exhaustion. In September, the city council marched the survivors to a shrine of Saint Vitus, and the dancing finally stopped. Historians still argue about why. One theory blamed a mould on rye bread. Medical historian John Waller rejects that, because rye wasn't a staple there and the mould causes symptoms nobody recorded. The leading idea now is mass hysteria in a city crushed by famine and disease. A whole town, dancing through a nightmare.

segments.heading: Vikings were in America in exactly 1021
segments.text: Vikings were living in North America in the year 1021, and we know that exact year because of a storm on the Sun. The Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada, was found in the 1960s, but nobody could say exactly when it was occupied. Then, in 2021, a team led by Michael Dee at the University of Groningen published a study in the journal Nature. In the year 993, a huge solar storm hit the Earth and left a spike of radioactive carbon in every tree growing that year. The team found that spike in logs from the Viking settlement, logs that had been cut with metal tools no native people in America used. They counted the rings from the spike out to the bark: twenty-eight. So the trees were felled in 1021. That's four hundred and seventy-one years before Columbus. The Vikings beat him to America by almost five centuries, and the Sun kept the receipt.

segments.heading: Tutankhamun was buried with a dagger from space
segments.text: King Tutankhamun was buried with a dagger made of metal from outer space. When Howard Carter unwrapped the pharaoh's mummy in 1925, he found an iron dagger lying on the boy king's right thigh. That alone was strange. Tutankhamun died around thirteen twenty-three BC, and Egyptians didn't learn to smelt iron from ore until roughly a thousand years later. In 2016, researchers from the Polytechnic University of Milan, the University of Pisa and the Egyptian Museum in Cairo scanned the blade with an X-ray fluorescence device, without touching it. The iron contained nearly eleven percent nickel and a trace of cobalt, a mix that is only found in meteorites. It closely matched a meteorite that fell near Marsa Matruh, on Egypt's coast. The Egyptians of that era even had a name for the stuff: iron from the sky. The most famous pharaoh in history went into the afterlife holding a piece of a fallen star.

outro: So that's a polar bear fishing in the Thames, a city that jacked itself out of the mud, and a pharaoh buried with a blade from space. Which one are you going to drop into conversation first? Tell me in the comments. There's a new fact here every evening.
description:
Ten history facts that sound made up but are completely true: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids, the fax machine is older than the telephone, Chicago lifted its entire downtown with screw jacks, and a polar bear once fished in the River Thames on a leash. We finish with the 2016 discovery that Tutankhamun was buried holding a dagger forged from a meteorite. Every fact is checked against a museum, a university or a major newspaper; the sources are listed below.
Which one surprised you most?
